thread.title: Apple’s Cook Has Pointed Advice for Facebook’s Zuckerberg

author: Jon Swartz
title: Apple’s Cook Has Pointed Advice for Facebook’s Zuckerberg

organizations.name: cook has pointed advice for facebook’s zuckerberg apple

text:
Apple CEO Tim Cook broke from Silicon Valley protocol when he criticized Mark Zuckerberg and Facebook (FB) in unusually blunt terms over its privacy flap.
Illustration: TIMOTHY A. CLARY/AFP/Getty Images "We could make a ton of money if we monetized our customers, if our customers were our product,” Cook told MSNBC and Recode in an interview set to air April 6. “We’ve elected not to do that.… We’re not going to traffic in your personal life. Privacy to us is a human right, a civil liberty.”
Echoing remarks he made in Beijing last week, Cook went so far as to advocate regulation of Facebook . “I think the best regulation is no regulation, is self-regulation,” he said. “However, I think we’re beyond that here.”
While Cook's pointed comments are consistent with his long-held views, they are also strategic. As Facebook and other social-media companies sink deeper into controversy over how they accumulate and share the personal information of billions of people, other tech companies like Apple (AAPL) may feel the need to make distinctions in how they use consumer data .
For years, Apple's top honcho has made the distinction between its business model—it sells products to customers for a profit—and that of internet platforms such as Facebook and Alphabet's Google (GOOGL) that are “gobbling up everything they can learn about you and trying to monetize it,” Cook said in 2015 .
Cook's stinging comments are the latest aimed at the embattled Zuckerberg, who faces increasing pressure to testify before Congress and the real possibility of regulation from U.S. and European lawmakers. The Federal Trade Commission says it has opened an investigation into Facebook.
Facebook says it is taking steps to tighten privacy settings, including curbing information it exchanges with third-party data aggregators such as Acxiom (ACXM) and Experian (EXPN.UK) that collect and sell consumer data for advertisers.
"Third-party data brokers often obtain their data through questionable means and do not have a direct relationship with consumers," says Peter Reinhardt, CEO of customer-data platform Segment. "Removing these brokers is a no-brainer, as they add very little incremental value to advertisers and a lot of rightful scrutiny to Facebook."
Facebook has also redesigned security settings so its 2.13 billion members can control what personal information the social network and third-party apps keep. A new "Access Your Information" button lets people delete anything from their profiles or timelines they no longer want, the company says.
